memoryText: Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass.
readingInstruction: Today there is no new reading. This week you finished the book of Joshua and began Judges. You read about the land being divided, the cities of refuge, and Joshua’s farewell, and then you watched the nation begin to unravel. Take a moment today to hold both together: a God who never fails, and a people who often do.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Joshua 21:45 is the hinge between two books. It closes the story of Joshua with a statement of God’s perfect faithfulness, and it throws a bright light on the sadness of Judges that follows.

“Not one word.” Not most, not nearly all. The promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and renewed to Moses and Joshua, had been kept in full. After centuries of slavery, wandering, and war, the record says nothing has failed.

“Of all the good promises.” The word “good” reminds us that God’s promises are not threats. They are gifts. He promised a land, rest, victory, and presence, and he gave them.

“That the LORD had made to the house of Israel.” The promises were made to a people, and they were kept for a people. They were also kept for the world, because through this people came the Messiah.

“All came to pass.” The statement is complete. Whatever Israel did or did not do, the LORD was faithful.

This verse will be tested immediately by Judges, where Israel is unfaithful and suffers for it. But God does not fail even then. Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 1:20 make the point: “All the promises of God find their Yes in him.” Every promise God has made is secured in Christ. Carry this verse into the week. When you wonder whether God will keep his word to you, remember that he has never failed.
weekInReview:
This week you walked through a long arc. You sang Psalm 23 and rested in the shepherd. You read the remaining tribal allotments and Joshua’s rebuke to those who delayed possessing the land. You studied the cities of refuge, the cities of the Levites, and the near-war over the altar by the Jordan, and you saw how Phinehas resolved it by asking first. You read Joshua’s farewell at Shechem, with its great challenge, “Choose this day whom you will serve,” and the sober reminder that no one is able to serve a holy God in his own strength. Then you opened Judges. You saw the incomplete conquest, the generation that did not know the LORD, and the repeating cycle of sin and rescue. You met Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, and then Deborah, Barak, and Jael, and heard the song of victory.

The week held a sharp contrast: God’s faithfulness is complete, and his people’s faithfulness is not.
reflectionQuestions: What is your “Shiloh”? Joshua asked the tribes how long they would put off taking what God had given. Is there something you have been waiting on, such as a step of obedience, a conversation, a calling, or a discipline? What is the first small step, and when will you take it?

How does Joshua’s statement, “You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God,” point you to Jesus? The people were confident they could keep the covenant, and they could not. Christ kept it perfectly on our behalf, and he gives his Spirit to write the law on our hearts. What changes for you when you stop trying to serve God in your own strength and start from what Christ has done?

Whom are you passing the faith on to? Judges 2:10 describes a generation that “did not know the LORD or the work that he had done.” Think of one younger person in your life, such as a child, a niece, a friend, or a fellow church member. What is one story of God’s faithfulness you could tell them this week?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that not one of his promises has failed.
Thank Christ in whom every promise is yes.
Confess any distrust, and rest in his faithfulness.
